content:
sam: Heads up — noticed a spike in outbound connections from the async Python SDK during our concurrency perf run after we rolled 1.4.0. CPU fine but connection count grows and never drops, hits socket limits.

elaine: Do you have a tiny repro we can try? sounds like session/client lifecycle misuse but want to confirm.

sam: Yep, minimal repro below (using the redwood async client). Repro runs in GH action when we spin 50 tasks.

sam: ```python
import asyncio
from redwood import AsyncClient

async def worker(i):
    client = AsyncClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")
    await client.complete("echo %d" % i)
    # no aclose here in the failing app

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*[worker(i) for i in range(50)])

asyncio.run(main())
```

sam: After ~1000 requests the test machine runs out of FDs. Metric: ephemeral tcp sockets in TIME_WAIT and many ESTABLISHED to api.redwood.com.

elaine: That pattern allocates a new TCP/session per task. Before 1.4 we had internal pooling that reused connectors; maybe the connector change in the new http backend removed reuse when client isn't closed.

elaine: Quick question — does your real app create a single client per process or spin up per request?

sam: Real app tried to reuse one client per worker process, but in the repro we accidentally constructed clients inside tasks to mimic bug. We saw both patterns fail in load test (maybe because of event loop / thread boundary reuse).

todd: Two things to check: 1) ensure client is awaited on close (.aclose()) or used as async context manager; 2) if you're reusing clients across threads or different event loops that can break connection pools.

todd: Example recommended pattern:

sam: ```python
from redwood import AsyncClient
client = AsyncClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")
# reuse this client for the lifetime of the process
# when shutting down: await client.aclose()
```

sophia: Thanks for the report, Sam. I dug into the SDK change: we swapped the underlying connector in 1.4.0 to support edge TLS options, but we forgot to port the async connector's global pool keying — so if you instantiate multiple clients on the same loop we created distinct connectors that didn't share the same TCP connector cache, and closing behavior was a no-op in some edge cases.

sophia: I've got a branch with a fix that restores pool sharing and ensures AsyncClient.aclose is idempotent. Pushing PR now. Can you run your GH workflow against benji/fix-async-pool-1769?

ci-bot: CI run queued: https://ci.example.com/runs/4672 — tests + integration load smoke (may take ~12m).

sam: Running it now on the same machine. Will paste results.

elaine: Also, as a short-term mitigation, use a module-level singleton client or an async context manager in workers. We'll add a note to the docs about avoiding per-request client instantiation for high concurrency.

sam: CI passed the unit tests on the branch but load still showed a small leak reduced ~90% — nice improvement. Attaching flame graphs and netstat diff later.

sophia: Perfect — can you include the netstat diff? I want to ensure TIME_WAIT vs ESTABLISHED behavior is fixed. If you see stray ESTABLISHED sockets after client.aclose that’s a different issue.

sam: Netstat diff: before -> after: ESTABLISHED down from ~480 -> ~12 after our patch. TIME_WAIT still exists briefly but decays quickly.

todd: Great. Let's ship the patch into a 1.4.1 hotfix. Sophia, can you add a small regression test that spins up 100 concurrent tasks creating+closing clients and asserts FD usage doesn't grow unbounded?

sophia: Yep will add test + a doc note about recommended process lifecycle for AsyncClient. Also adding a linter comment in the example that warns against per-request instantiation.

sam: Thanks folks — saved us from hitting infra limits in staging. Leaving this thread open until patch lands in PyPI and we confirm the dedicated cluster run.

ci-bot: PR #889 opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/python-sdk/pull/889 — includes test, fix, and docs.

sam: Will smoke test tomorrow morning and post results. :thumbsup:
